silu-051.title: Ice returns and the sea drains off the shelves
silu-051.text: The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian. In the middle of the age, growing ice locked away seawater. The oceans pulled back in a major regression, a retreat of the sea from the coasts. Vast new land lay exposed. Life moved in fast: plants and mats of cyanobacteria, the photosynthesizing microbes, quickly colonized the bare ground, pushing plant diversification further. The same cold snap is tied to {{ref:silu-054}}, the extinction that followed.

silu-062.title: The Šilalė event strikes the conodonts
silu-062.text: Early in the Pridoli, conodonts suffered another extinction, the Šilalė event. It is marked by a negative carbon isotope excursion, a sudden shift in the chemistry of carbon. That shift is traced from cores in Lithuania to the Appalachian Basin of North America. While conodonts declined, brachiopods grew in diversity and abundance. The crisis coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year cycle in the shape of Earth's orbit.

devo-001.title: Jawed fishes take over in the Age of Fishes
devo-001.text:
The Devonian earned its popular name, the Age of Fishes, honestly. Jawed vertebrates had appeared in the late Ordovician, but only now did they become common. Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks.

The family tree had already branched. By about 419 million years ago jawed fishes had split into three lines. They were the armored placoderms, the bony fishes, and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish. Both cartilaginous and bony fishes diversified through the period and played a large role in Devonian seas. Among the bony fishes, the lobe-finned forms, such as coelacanths and lungfish, were the most diverse. That detail matters, because the lobe-fins are the group from which four-limbed animals would later come.

devo-009.title: Oxygen climbs toward modern levels
devo-009.text: Early in the Silurian, the air held only about 13% of today's oxygen level. By the end of the Devonian it was near modern. Early in the Devonian oxygen was still fairly low, possibly about half of modern values. The climb from 470 to 400 million years ago is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. It is explained by early plants trapping organic carbon in sediments, so that it could not use up oxygen by decaying. As plants spread over the continents, they buried more carbon still. The richer air may have favored vertebrates able to breathe it, helping push tetrapods onto land.

devo-072.title: Tree roots teach rivers to meander
devo-072.text: Roots changed the shape of rivers. By 370 million years ago, abundant trees such as Archaeopteris bound soils firmly. Rivers switched from mostly braided, splitting into many channels, to mostly meandering, swinging in single looping channels.

devo-084.title: The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian
devo-084.text:
Two ash beds in Poland pin down a catastrophe. They bracket a black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 million years ago. That shale records the Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, which closed the Famennian.

The toll was heavy. It killed the last placoderms and the stromatoporoid reef sponges. It left Proetida as the only trilobite order and nearly wiped out the ammonoids. Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages. One estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though land plants were spared.

The likely trigger was cold. Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian marked the start of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age and may have driven the losses. Other proposed causes pile up: anoxia from high plankton productivity, volcanism in Kola and Timan-Pechora, ozone loss hinted at by malformed spores, and even a nearby supernova. None is settled, and several may have acted together.

carb-027.title: The ice age tightens its grip
carb-027.text:
Around 330 million years ago, an ice sheet kilometers thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole. It belonged to the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. That phase began between 335 and 330 million years ago, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and carbon dioxide fell.

The onset reshaped coastlines everywhere. Sea level fell worldwide, leaving unconformities, gaps in the rock record lasting millions of years. Ice spread from up to 30 centers across Gondwana. Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells, and the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian.

The ice left thick evidence. Its deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group. Those piles of scraped and dumped rock record ice that came and went for tens of millions of years.

carb-033.title: Amniotes and the egg that left the water
carb-033.text:
An egg that dries out is a dead egg. One tetrapod lineage solved that problem. It evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land, and these animals are the amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

When they arose is disputed. Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 million years ago, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 million years ago. Another account puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous. Clawed footprints from the Tournaisian of Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks. If so, amniotes go back to the start of the period or earlier. Researchers have not settled the question.

What is clearer is how they took over. Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes rose in their place.

carb-046.title: Equatorial Pangaea dries out
carb-046.text: The swamps did not last forever. Toward the end of the Carboniferous, Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier, beginning a dry trend that lasted into the Triassic. After about 318 million years ago, seasons swung often between humid and arid. A cycle of drying began in the late Moscovian, with abrupt changes in animal life. Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained, more stable landscapes. Weaker weathering in the drier climate even lowered the seawater strontium-isotope ratio. Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling carbon dioxide and low-latitude aridity brought a permanent shift to seasonally dry woodland.

carb-053.title: Synapsids and sauropsids part ways
carb-053.text: Every mammal and every bird traces back to a single fork in the amniote family tree. Amniotes split into two lines: synapsids, the mammal lineage, and sauropsids, the line of reptiles and birds. Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 million years ago and the first synapsids around 318 million years ago. The earliest fossils of both date to about 313 million years ago. Synapsid pelycosaurs appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate land for some 40 million years. By the period's end, amniotes had diversified into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

perm-006.title: The Gondwanide orogeny folds the south
perm-006.text: South Africa's Cape Fold Belt and Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana are the folded remains of one Permian mountain belt. Mountain building deformed southern Gondwana, in what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea. Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two. In South Africa, folding entered a new phase from about 260 million years ago. By then the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, had spread.

perm-021.title: The Skagerrak large igneous province
perm-021.text: Magma spread over at least 0.5 million km² around today's Skagerrak strait, 297 ± 4 million years ago. This large igneous province reached the Oslo and Skagerrak grabens, south-western Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea. It is the oldest of a series tied to the African superplume, a vast upwelling deep in the mantle. Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic followed. With Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province, it is tied to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 million years ago.

perm-022.title: The Central Pangean Mountains at their height
perm-022.text: In the early Permian, a mountain range along the equator rivaled today's Himalayas. The Central Pangean Mountains rose where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies. Those collisions began about 340 million years ago and ended about 295 million years ago. Their western part, the Appalachians, was uplifted then. The range cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later helped lay down Europe's Zechstein salt. Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian, spreading sandstone and conglomerate across Europe. The Appalachians, Ouachitas, Atlas and Bohemian Massif are its remnants.

perm-030.title: The Artinskian warming melts the ice
perm-030.text: When the Permian began, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age was at its peak. It did not stay that way. Ice sheets shrank from the late Sakmarian on. By 287 million years ago temperatures had risen and the south polar ice cap had retreated, in the Artinskian Warming Event. Glaciers clung on only in eastern Australia's uplands. Around 285.1 million years ago, orbital cycles stopped driving ice growth and began driving marine anoxia and aridity instead, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse. As the glaciers receded, seas rose and the continental interiors dried out.

perm-048.title: Olson's Extinction
perm-048.text: Most pelycosaur lineages vanished around 273 million years ago, long before the end-Permian crisis. Edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out near the Kungurian–Roadian boundary, while caseids and therapsids diversified. Temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply afterward, and extinction rates in fish rose. Extreme environments in Kansas, combining heat and acidic waters, coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause. This proposed extinction is contested. A review of Kungurian and Roadian beds found the turnover real. Some authors argue it reflects poor sampling or gradual change, and the timing of Olson's Gap is disputed.

perm-071.title: The Kupferschiefer, a copper-bearing black shale
perm-071.text: A layer usually only 30–60 cm thick spreads over 600,000 square km across six countries. The Kupferschiefer formed about 257 million years ago in the enclosed Zechstein basin. Oxygen-free water there laid down a black shale and marl holding up to 30% organic matter. Mineral-rich groundwater later formed sulfide ores in it. It became one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199 AD.

perm-077.title: Salt fills the Delaware Basin
perm-077.text: Tectonics pinched the Hovey Channel shut. The deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico was cut off from the sea, and its brines grew ever saltier. Up to 91 m of finely layered gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep. Thick halite of the Salado followed. By the end of the Ochoan, the basin had filled to the top of the Capitan Reef and was mostly dry land.
